newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania in crisis talks amid Europe warnings.
newsitem.headline: Albania in crisis talks amid Europe warnings.

text.p: Albania's politicians met for crisis talks on Saturday to end a row over elections while Western governments warned that compromise must be found.

The elections are aimed at bringing order back to the chaotic Balkan state, engulfed by rioting and violence earlier this year after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which thousands lost their life savings.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino gathered the parties of his national unity government after most of them threatened to boycott the vote over election laws they say favour President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
On Friday Berisha went ahead and called the vote for June 29, despite the threatened boycott. Fino had also met Berisha late on Friday to discuss the elections.

The same day the European Union issued the latest of a string of warnings to the Albanians that if a compromise was not found to allow free and fair elections, then international aid might be withheld.

"Should political stalemate not be overcome within the next days and elections not take place on June 29, the EU, in close cooperation with the international community as a whole, may be forced to reconsider its efforts of support in Albania," it said in a statement issued by the Dutch government.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and current chairman of top European security body the OSCE, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, also on Friday urged compromise.
In what was turning out to be a tough process, the talks broke up after four hours and were to reconvene in the evening.
The second-largest party, the Socialists, insisted the boycott threat stood if changes to the law were not agreed.
"We are not in a hurry to declare now that we will not join the elections of June 29," said Socialist leader Fatos Nano.
"But if nothing changes I am afraid not only the political forums of the parties which take decisions but also a striking majority of Albanians...will not join this process," he said.
All parties were present at the Fino meeting, including the Democratic Party.

European envoy Franz Vranitzky, leaving Albania on Friday after a fifth mission in which he failed once again to solve the polical crisis, had urged politicians to compromise and said the international community may withdraw assistance.
Vranitzky seemed to win a compromise Thursday by persuading parliament, dominated by the Democrats, to amend election laws.
But the other parties were unhappy with the new legislation and maintained the boycott threat.
Fino heads a nine-party Government of National Reconciliation which Berisha was forced to install in March as anger about the pyramid schemes boiled over into insurrection.
Independent newspaper Koha Jone said Fino received the backing of Vranitzy, who asked him to stay in office despite the tension created by the election wrangle.
The Socialists pulled out of elections in May 1996, which gave the Democrats a landslide win but which international observers criticised for being deeply flawed.
The other parties also want more seats decided by proportional representation to favour smaller parties while the Democrats favour a system of greater majority voting.
